lines.text: Today your pages get lists, links to other pages and pictures, the way real websites do.
The ul tag makes a bulleted list, and the ol tag makes a numbered list.
Each item goes inside its own li tag.
Use numbers when the order matters, like recipe steps.
The a tag turns words into a link you can click.
Its href part holds the web address to visit.
The words between the tags are what people click.
The img tag shows a picture, and its src part says where the picture lives.
An img tag is special, because it has no closing tag.
It just sits in the page like a stamp.
Alt text is a short description of the image.
Screen readers read it aloud for people who cannot see the picture.
It also shows up if the picture fails to load.
Pictures belong to the people who made them.
Use your own drawings, free placeholder images or free pictures that allow sharing.
Always write who made it under the picture.
The ul tag wraps the whole list, and each li tag holds one item.
The browser adds a round bullet in front of every item for us.
Swap ul for ol and the bullets become numbers.
If you add a new step in the middle, the browser renumbers everything for you.
The href holds the address, and the word mangoes is what you click.
Links are what join millions of pages into one giant web.
The src says where the picture lives, and the alt describes it in words.
If the picture cannot load, or someone uses a screen reader, the alt text tells them what it shows.
Two problems here. The list items never close, and the picture has no alt text.
Close every li tag, and always describe your picture with alt text.
Great work! Let’s remember what we learned.
Now build along, then try the challenges. You’ve got this!
